sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: By late 1915 the German chief of staff, Erich von Falkenhayn, believed Germany could not win by military strength alone. He planned to defeat France before British forces were fully deployed, hoping a major French defeat would push its politicians toward peace. In the memorandum he later published as his Christmas 1915 appreciation, he named Britain the central enemy, judged that an advance on Moscow would achieve nothing, and saw France weakened almost to the limit of what it could endure.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Verdun was chosen in December 1915. Its forts had been stripped of guns in August 1915, its supply routes were limited, and the city combined military value with national pride: French leaders declared that morale would not survive its loss.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Imperial War Museums describes Falkenhayn's concept as using more than 1,200 guns to destroy French units on ground they had to retake, while committing German infantry sparingly. The memorandum states the idea in his own terms: attack an objective the French would defend with their last man, so that France would bleed to death whether or not Germany took it, in a limited operation whose tempo Germany could control; of Belfort and Verdun, Verdun was to be preferred. The French aimed simply to hold Verdun.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The fortress city lay on the River Meuse, ringed by 19 forts, of which Douaumont was the largest and highest. Heights on the east (right) bank dominated the area; the Mort-Homme and Hill 304 lay on the west bank. A single road from Bar-le-Duc carried most French supply.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The German Fifth Army attacked under Crown Prince Wilhelm, with General Schmidt von Knobelsdorf an influential adviser. The French Second Army was commanded from 26 February by Philippe Pétain and later by Robert Nivelle, under Joffre as commander-in-chief.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: French positions north of the city were thin. Lieutenant-Colonel Driant, who had warned of the weak defences, held woods in the path of the attack with about 1,200 light infantry; only around a hundred survived unhurt.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: A massive bombardment opened the battle on 21 February 1916, and Fort Douaumont fell on 25 February. Germany attacked the west bank from 6 March, took Fort Vaux on 7 June and reached Fort Souville on 11–12 July before being pushed back. French counteroffensives retook Douaumont on 24 October and Vaux in November, and the battle ended in December.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Pétain defended in depth with mutually supporting strongpoints, rotated divisions through the battle in a system called the noria and greatly increased French artillery. Crown Prince Wilhelm's staff, by contrast, made seizing ground the priority rather than Falkenhayn's limited concept.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Once both armies fought for ground rather than to destroy the other's units, losses fell equally on both. The Somme offensive from late June then forced Germany to reduce its effort at Verdun and let Nivelle attack.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: France held Verdun and recovered Douaumont, Vaux and much of the lost ground. Falkenhayn's plan to destroy the French army had failed.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Verdun's losses, added to those of the Somme, created a German manpower crisis. In France the battle became the national symbol of the Great War. Nine villages were destroyed and never rebuilt, and the Douaumont Ossuary holds the remains of about 130,000 soldiers.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: An attritional plan depends on controlling the objective. When commanders pursue ground for its own sake, the attacker can suffer as heavily as the defender.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Falkenhayn's postwar claim that he meant to bleed the French army white is debated; other readings stress the capture of the town or drawing in Allied reserves. The Christmas memorandum that states the claim is printed in his own memoir of 1920, from which German History in Documents and Images takes its text, and its editors read it chiefly as a strategy against Britain. The sources differ on the start of the bombardment (4 a.m. or 7.15 a.m.), the end date (15 or 18 December) and when Pétain left (late April or May).

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Mémorial de Verdun gives a detailed French chronology, logistics and memory. Imperial War Museums gives the strategic concept and the changing German conduct of the battle. Falkenhayn's Christmas memorandum, in Jeffrey Verhey's translation, gives the German commander's stated reasoning as he published it after the war.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Germany's war plan sent the main blow against France first; Nagornaja explains that the German General Staff expected Russia's slow mobilisation to let a single army hold the east until victory in the west. To ease German pressure on France, the Russian commander-in-chief, Grand Duke Nicholas, urged his First and Second Armies into East Prussia before they were fully ready. General Zhilinsky had earlier pledged to France that Russia would field 800,000 men by the 15th day of mobilisation.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: With more than two-to-one superiority, a combined Russian attack could have destroyed the German Eighth Army. But the two army commanders, Rennenkampf and Samsonov, had quarrelled bitterly since the Russo-Japanese War. The invasion sent a stream of refugees west, and stories of Cossack atrocities spread through German public opinion.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Zhilinsky's plan had Rennenkampf's First Army attack from the east to draw the Germans on, while Samsonov's Second Army crossed the southern frontier two days later to cut them off from the Vistula. The Germans aimed to break the invasion.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The 80-km chain of the Masurian Lakes separated the two Russian armies, and the Königsberg fortifications narrowed Rennenkampf's approach. The Russians had left their own border country a barrier of poor railways and worse roads, which now slowed Samsonov.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Rennenkampf had six and a half infantry and five cavalry divisions; Samsonov ten infantry and three cavalry divisions, both under Zhilinsky. The German Eighth Army was commanded by Prittwitz, then by Hindenburg, appointed on 22 August, with Ludendorff as chief of staff and Max Hoffmann on the staff.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Rennenkampf crossed the frontier and pushed back much of the Eighth Army at Gumbinnen on 19–20 August. Samsonov's army, hurried on by Zhilinsky, reached the southern frontier tired, hungry and with its transport incomplete, and spread across a front of nearly 100 km.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 20 August Prittwitz spoke of retreating behind the Vistula, but his staff prepared a move against Samsonov's left; he was replaced two days later. The main battle was fought from 26 to 30 August around Allenstein. On 26 August François's I Corps attacked near Usdau, and on 27 August the Russian left broke. By 29 August the Germans held the road behind the Russian centre, which surrendered in the forests.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Hoffmann trusted Russian wireless orders sent uncoded, which his superiors suspected were a deception. Ludendorff took the risk of withdrawing almost everything from in front of Rennenkampf, leaving a cavalry screen, to strike both of Samsonov's flanks. Zhilinsky drove Samsonov forward and diverted Rennenkampf towards Königsberg.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: On 27 August the Russian left wing broke under bombardment before the German infantry attacked. François then turned east to Neidenburg, closing the line of retreat of the Russian centre.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Russian centre dissolved into exhausted groups that surrendered in large numbers. Samsonov, caught in the retreat, shot himself; Britannica places this early on 30 August, Rickard probably on 29 August. On 31 August Hindenburg thanked the Eighth Army in an order of the day, printed in German newspapers, announcing that the remnants of the Narew Army were fleeing south and that Rennenkampf's army had begun to retreat from Königsberg.

refs.locator: Planning and execution; Outcome and aftermath

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Reinforced from the west, the Germans drove Rennenkampf out of East Prussia in September. Britannica notes that they could not turn the victory into a strategic one, and that the corps sent east helped make possible the French recovery on the Marne; Nagornaja adds that a second Russian incursion followed in the winter of 1914–1915. For Russia the defeat was a heavy blow to morale, and a commission of inquiry examined its causes.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Two armies separated by terrain and unwilling to cooperate could be beaten one at a time. Uncoded radio gave the defender the knowledge to take great risks, and railways let it shift forces quickly.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Britannica gives Hoffmann chief credit for the design and François the essential role, and calls the double envelopment an afterthought rather than a planned second Cannae; Rickard notes that German commanders credited Hindenburg and Ludendorff, and the German History in Documents and Images editors call Ludendorff the architect while Hindenburg became the hero. Hindenburg named the battle after nearby Tannenberg rather than Allenstein, recasting it as revenge for the Teutonic Knights' defeat there in 1410; Nagornaja traces how the name and the idea of a second Cannae became a German national myth, while in Russia the defeat was explained as a sacrifice to save Paris or as Rennenkampf's treachery. Britannica blames Zhilinsky above all, Rickard Samsonov's own push. Dates differ by a day or two.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Britannica gives a detailed narrative and Rickard a short biography of Samsonov. Nagornaja's article for 1914-1918-online is brief on the fighting but traces the battle's place in German and Russian memory. Hindenburg's order of the day of 31 August, with the German History in Documents and Images introduction, is the victor's announcement; its figures for prisoners and booty are not used.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Leaders and the public on both sides expected a short war decided by a few great battles. The French offensive plan, Plan XVII, failed in Alsace and Lorraine and was soon abandoned, while the German right wing, following the Schlieffen Plan as modified by the younger Moltke, swept through Belgium. After the Battle of the Frontiers the French armies and the British Expeditionary Force fell back toward the Marne. Cochet stresses that the retreat never became a rout; the British stood at Mons and Le Cateau, and the French Fifth Army struck back at Guise.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Germany's plan depended on defeating France quickly. Moltke weakened his right wing by detaching divisions to besiege Maubeuge and Givet and to watch Antwerp, and on 25 August by sending troops to East Prussia. The French government left Paris for Bordeaux, and Paris prepared for a siege under its military governor, Gallieni. Coalition command rested on persuasion: on 5 September Joffre had to convince Field Marshal Sir John French to take part in the counter-attack.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Joffre decided to swing back his centre and left with Verdun as the pivot, form a fresh Sixth Army on his left and return to the offensive. His order of the day, written on 5 September and read to the troops on the 6th, told them to attack and, where they could not advance, to hold the ground they had taken. On 4 September Moltke abandoned the wide sweep beyond Paris for a narrower envelopment of the French centre and right, with his First and Second Armies turning to face any move from Paris.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The name is misleading: the fighting ran for about 300 kilometres, from Senlis to Verdun, and much of it lay far from the river. In the west were the Ourcq and the approaches to Paris; in the centre, the marshes of Saint-Gond and the height of Mondement; in the east, the ground around Verdun, which Cochet calls of capital importance as the hinge of the front. Britannica notes that rivers crossing the line of advance slowed the Allied push into the gap between the German armies.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Joffre commanded the French armies, from Maunoury's Sixth Army near Paris through Franchet d'Espèrey's Fifth and Foch's Ninth to the armies around Verdun, where General Coutanceau held the fortress. Sir John French's British Expeditionary Force fought alongside them but had to be persuaded rather than ordered. Moltke directed the German armies from distant headquarters in Luxembourg; Kluck's First, Bülow's Second and Hausen's Third Armies formed the right.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: By early September Kluck had wheeled inward east of Paris to help Bülow against the French Fifth Army, carrying his flank across the face of the Paris defences into the Marne valley. On 3 September, as the German First Army crossed the Marne, Gallieni saw what the wheel meant and readied Maunoury's Sixth Army to strike the exposed German right; he won Joffre's approval the next day, and Joffre ordered the whole left wing to turn and attack on 6 September.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Maunoury's army moved on 5 September and the general offensive began on the 6th. As pressure grew on his flank, Kluck drew first part and then the rest of his army west against Maunoury, opening a gap of about 48 kilometres between the First and Second Armies, covered only by cavalry. On the 8th Franchet d'Espèrey's Fifth Army widened it with a night attack. In the centre the main German effort fell on Foch's Ninth Army near the marshes of Saint-Gond; Mondement was retaken on the evening of the 9th. The German retreat began on 9 and 10 September, while fighting near Verdun went on until the 12th.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Three decisions shaped the battle. Joffre abandoned Plan XVII, moved troops by rail to build a new army on his left and returned to the offensive. Kluck, by wheeling inward before Paris was reached, exposed the German right to a counter-envelopment. Moltke, far from the front and out of touch with his armies, left the decisive judgement to his staff officer, Lieutenant Colonel Hentsch, whose decisions Cochet describes as going far beyond his rank.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The turning point came on 9 September. Reports of British columns advancing into the gap led Bülow to order his Second Army to retreat, and the First Army, whose local advantage over Maunoury was thereby nullified, fell back the same day. Hentsch, sent from Moltke's headquarters, persuaded Kluck that his position was exposed and that he should break off the fight.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The French and British threw back the German advance and ended German hopes of a quick and total victory in the west. For the Germans it was a strategic but not a tactical defeat: their right wing re-formed on the lower Aisne and the Chemin des Dames ridge, where trench warfare set in after Allied assaults later in September. The Allies could not exploit the gap fast enough to destroy the German armies.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The Allied pursuit was checked on the Aisne, and on 17 September Joffre formed a new army to get around the German flank, the beginning of the 'race to the sea'. Cochet sees the battle as the opening of total, industrial war: the human toll was enormous, junior officers fell in such numbers that lieutenants led companies, and the mourning that followed made a negotiated peace almost unthinkable. Charles Péguy was killed on 5 September and Alain-Fournier later in the month. French periodicals celebrated Joffre as the victor.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Railways let a defender move armies faster than an attacker could march, and Joffre's calm and 'iron grip', in Cochet's words, held beaten armies together. An advance that outruns its supplies and its commander's knowledge is fragile: Britannica stresses that the German armies outran their timetable and their supplies and that their high command lost touch with the front. Le Gall adds that the French army was already learning, digging and using trenches within weeks of charging in the open.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Credit for the counter-stroke is disputed: Britannica says the opportunity was perceived by Gallieni rather than Joffre, while Cochet calls the question pointless and credits Joffre, the only commander with a view of the whole front. The sources date the battle 6–12 or 6–11 September and give different numbers for the troops carried to the front in Paris taxis, though both treat the episode as real. Le Gall argues that the name 'Battle of the Marne', and its memory in France as a 'miracle', express a French national reading that leaves out much of the coalition's part.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: François Cochet's article for the French Ministry of the Armed Forces (in French) gives the French command view, the extent of the front and the human cost. Britannica gives the operational sequence from Mons to the Aisne and the German decisions. Erwan Le Gall's 1914-1918-online article covers coalition command, the learning curve of the French army and memory.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After the Marne and the stalemate on the Aisne, each side tried to turn the other's open northern flank, the 'race to the sea'. Castelnau's French flanking attempt came to a stop on the Somme by 24 September, and Maud'huy's new Tenth Army soon found itself struggling to hold Arras. The British Expeditionary Force moved north from the Aisne to shorten its communications with England, and Antwerp fell on 10 October.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Falkenhayn had taken over the German army after the Marne and tried to turn the tide in the West. Ypres mattered for its position and as a transport hub on the way to the Channel ports of Dunkirk and Calais. Joffre made Foch his deputy in the north to coordinate the Allied flanking move, while King Albert I declined to abandon the coast for an advance inland that he considered rash.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Germans meant to push through to Dunkirk and Calais, and for that they needed Ypres. On 14 October Falkenhayn planned a trap: one army would hold the expected Allied offensive while another, built from troops freed by the fall of Antwerp and four newly raised corps, swept down the Belgian coast to crush the Allied left. The Allies meant to make a third attempt to turn the German flank by attacking from Ypres toward Menin.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Ypres lies in western Flanders. East of the town the Menin road ran through Gheluvelt; to the south lay the Messines Ridge, Wytschaete and the high ground of Mount Kemmel; to the north the Yser river and canal ran to the sea at Nieuport. The Allied trenches were crude, giving cover against bullets but little protection against artillery.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The German Fourth Army under Albrecht, Duke of Württemberg, and the Sixth Army, later joined by an ad hoc force under General von Fabeck, faced the British Expeditionary Force under Sir John French, a French Eighth Army forming beside it, and the Belgian army on the Yser. Lieutenant General Sir Douglas Haig commanded the British I Corps. Foch coordinated the Allied effort for Joffre and committed French reinforcements, but had to persuade rather than command the Belgians.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: The Allied corps arrived piecemeal from the south. The British deployed between La Bassée and Ypres, where they joined Rawlinson's IV Corps; beyond them the French Eighth Army was forming, and the Belgians held the line of the Yser to the sea. Falkenhayn held back the troops that had been pursuing the Belgians so as not to alarm the Allied command.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 19 October Sir John French ordered his left to attack toward Menin, just as the German offensive opened on the 20th; for at least a day he believed he was attacking while his troops were barely holding. From 25 October the Belgians began flooding the Yser valley, and on the 29th King Albert ordered the sluices at Nieuport opened. Fabeck's attack drove the British from Zandvoorde on 30 October and took Gheluvelt on the 31st before a counter-attack retook the village; Messines Ridge fell on 1 and 2 November. A last attack on 11 November, led by the Prussian Guard astride the Menin road, broke into the Nonne Bosschen wood and was thrown back.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Falkenhayn sought a decision in the West with a coastal trap and repeated assaults; Afflerbach writes that the bloody setback at Ypres permanently damaged his reputation. On the Allied side, Britannica calls the battle a 'soldiers' battle': French and Foch misread the situation for days, and local commanders and units decided the outcome. King Albert's refusal to leave the coast, and his decision to flood the Yser, secured the Allied left.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Three moments decided the battle. The flooding of the Yser from 29 October forced German divisions back and secured the Allied left. On 31 October a counter-attack organised by Brigadier General FitzClarence and delivered by the 2nd Worcestershire Regiment retook Gheluvelt and closed the break in the British line, while French reinforcements sent by Foch held other crises. The failure of the Prussian Guard on 11 November effectively ended the battle.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The German offensive was brought to a standstill and Ypres stayed in Allied hands, though only as an exposed salient. Neither side broke through, and both settled into the trench warfare that marked the rest of the war on the Western Front. In Britain the battle was celebrated as a victory.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Both sides suffered heavy losses, and the British casualties effectively destroyed Britain's highly trained pre-war army. The Germans turned to the defensive in the West and sent available troops to Russia; in November Falkenhayn concluded that decisive victory was possible neither in the East nor in the West. Ypres became a centre of remembrance, and on the German side Käthe Kollwitz's sculpture The Grieving Parents was inspired by the loss of her youngest son at First Ypres.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Even crude entrenchments, defended with rapid rifle, machine-gun and artillery fire, could stop attackers who had more men and more guns. Mobile war in the west ended less by design than because every flanking attempt met a defender who arrived in time. The Belgian inundation showed how a defender could turn the ground itself into an obstacle.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Jones notes that the historiography still rests largely on the British, French and German official histories, and that recent work stresses the many nations involved. The sources frame the battle differently: Britannica as a soldiers' battle decided by personal valour more than by high command, Jones as a demonstration of the strength of entrenched defence. Loss figures differ between accounts because they count different periods and stretches of front.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Britannica gives the detailed sequence from the race to the sea to the Prussian Guard attack. Spencer Jones's 1914-1918-online article on the battles of Ypres gives the overview, the significance of the battle and its place in remembrance. Holger Afflerbach's 1914-1918-online biography gives Falkenhayn's view, and Britannica's article on the Marne gives the start of the race to the sea.

phases.title: Meeting engagement

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After the First Battle of Ypres, British and French troops held an exposed salient around the city, a sector of incessant trench warfare. Gas had already been tried without success: French rifle grenades filled with tear gas from August 1914, and German shells filled with irritants at Neuve-Chapelle in October 1914 and at Bolimów in January 1915. The Hague Peace Conference of 1899 had asked nations to abstain from projectiles whose object was to spread asphyxiating or deleterious gases.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: In 1915 the Germans stood mostly on the defensive in the West. Their spring attack at Ypres was meant to cover the transfer of German divisions to the Eastern Front for a new offensive in Galicia, to shorten their line by reducing the salient, and to test chlorine as a weapon. Ypres was the last major Belgian town in Allied hands and protected the French Channel ports.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Jones stresses that the German objectives were strictly limited and did not include the capture of Ypres itself. Britannica describes a first move to secure a bridgehead across the Yser canal, followed by attacks southward in echelon to roll the British line back west of Ypres.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The attack fell on the northern face of the salient, opposite Langemarck, where British, French and Belgian forces met. Behind the line lay the Yser canal, the village of St. Julien and the low rise of Pilckem Ridge; Kitcheners' Wood stood west of St. Julien. Gas released from cylinders needed the wind to blow toward the Allied lines.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The German Fourth Army under Albrecht, Duke of Württemberg, faced, from south to north, Smith-Dorrien's British Second Army, which included the 1st Canadian Division under Alderson, the French 45th (Algerian) and 87th Territorial Divisions under General Putz, and the Belgian 6th Division. Fritz Haber directed the German release of gas. Foch ordered the French counter-attack after the line broke.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: On 14 April British and French headquarters received detailed information that the Germans meant to release gas from cylinders opposite Langemarck, but while the troops were warned to expect an attack, they were not told about the gas. The German assault troops gathered unseen in Houthulst Forest. Mines at St. Eloi and Hill 60 and the bombardment of Ypres from 19 April drew Allied attention elsewhere.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: At 5 p.m. on 22 April a greenish-yellow cloud of chlorine drifted onto the French divisions, whose men suffocated or fled. By nightfall the Germans had crossed the canal and taken Pilckem Ridge, leaving the left flank of the Canadian Division exposed. The Canadians shifted to cover the gap and counter-attacked at Kitcheners' Wood that night; British and Canadian counter-attacks on the 23rd had almost no artillery support. On the 24th a second gas attack struck the Canadians directly. The fighting then became a see-saw of attack and counter-attack until 25 May.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: The German command treated gas as a means to limited ends and had no substantial reserves ready to exploit a breakthrough; Jones writes that the scale of the first success apparently surprised the Germans and that they missed a rare chance to press further. On the Allied side, the decision not to pass the warning about gas down to the troops left them without any protection. The Allies answered the breach with hasty counter-attacks that cost heavily for little ground.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The first night decided the battle. The gap was open, but no German troops were ready to pass through it, and Canadians, gassed Algerian survivors and reserve battalions formed a flank. By the morning of 23 April a continuous line had been built from the Canadian left to the canal. The Canadians held through the second gas attack on the 24th, giving ground slowly while British reinforcements were rushed forward.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Germans gained about four kilometres of important ground and narrowed the salient, but Ypres stayed in Allied hands. German artillery now reached the city and reduced it to rubble. The Canadian Division earned a reputation as tough and dependable troops.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Gas warfare spread to every army: the British released chlorine at Loos in September 1915, phosgene followed late in 1915 and mustard gas in 1917, and the armies raced to develop masks and respirators. Jones attributes the heavy Allied losses at Ypres mainly to the initial lack of protection against gas. After the war gas remained a focus of arms control, leading to the Geneva Protocol of 1925. During the battle the Canadian doctor John McCrae wrote 'In Flanders Fields'.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A new weapon used for surprise can open a gap, but without a plan and reserves to exploit it the advantage passes, the defender adapts and the surprise does not come twice. Gas became a permanent hazard for which every army had to organise, from masks and alarms to medical services, and the Canadian War Museum notes that masks and precautions reduced the German advantage.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources date the start to 21 or 22 April; Britannica and Jones run the battle to 25 May, while the Canadian War Museum's account of the Canadian part covers 22 to 25 April. They give different quantities for the chlorine released. Faith quotes the 1899 Hague declaration, which concerned projectiles; at Ypres the gas was released from cylinders, and the sources read do not settle whether the attack breached it. Canadian accounts centre on the Canadian stand, while Britannica also records the parts played by Algerian, French, British and Belgian troops.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Britannica gives the forces, the warning, the gas attack and the counter-attacks in detail. Spencer Jones's 1914-1918-online article on the battles of Ypres gives the German aims and the result. The Canadian War Museum's pages on Second Ypres and on poison gas give the Canadian part and the spread of gas warfare, and Thomas I. Faith's 1914-1918-online article on gas warfare gives the earlier attempts, the Hague declaration and the later development of gas.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Weakened by territorial losses between 1911 and 1913, the Ottoman government of the Committee of Union and Progress, led by Enver, invited German advisers under General Otto Liman von Sanders to reform its army. The empire made a secret alliance with Germany and mobilised in August 1914; after a naval sortie against Russia's Black Sea coast it declared war on the Entente on 31 October 1914.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: By early 1915 the Western Front was deadlocked. In January Britain agreed to stage a demonstration against the Ottoman Empire to relieve the Russians, and Winston Churchill, First Lord of the Admiralty, championed forcing the Dardanelles. Kitchener, Secretary of State for War, agreed to support a joint offensive.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Allies sought to force the straits, bring Constantinople under the guns of the fleet, knock the Ottoman Empire out of the war and open Russia's shipping route between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean. The landing force was to seize the Gallipoli peninsula and the Kilid Bahr plateau above the forts so that the fleet could pass. Success depended on a quick victory.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The Dardanelles is a channel about 61 kilometres long that separates the Gallipoli peninsula from the Asian shore. The beaches were small and separated, overlooked by high ground: the Sari Bair range and Chunuk Bair above Anzac Cove, Achi Baba above Cape Helles, and the Anafarta hills behind Suvla Bay. Harsh, scrub-covered slopes and valleys favoured defenders on the heights.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: General Sir Ian Hamilton's Mediterranean Expeditionary Force combined British, Indian, Australian, New Zealand, Newfoundland and French troops and a Royal Navy division; the Australians and New Zealanders formed the ANZAC corps under Birdwood. Liman von Sanders directed the Ottoman defence through the Fifth Army; Esat Pasha's III Corps held the peninsula, Cevat Pasha commanded the fortified area of Çanakkale, and Lieutenant Colonel Mustafa Kemal commanded the 19th Division.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: An Allied fleet bombarded the forts from 19 February 1915, and on 18 March an attempt to force the narrows failed when ships struck mines. Troops gathered at Mudros on the island of Lemnos. Hamilton planned landings at Cape Helles by the British 29th Division and near Gaba Tepe by the ANZAC, with feints by the Royal Naval Division at Bulair and by the French at Kum Kale on the Asian shore.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 25 April the ANZAC landed at Ariburnu, the beach later called Anzac Cove, and the British at Helles; both were held to shallow beachheads. British attacks toward Krithia in April, May and June failed, as did a large Ottoman night attack on the Anzac lines on 19–20 May, after which a ceasefire allowed the dead to be buried. In August a new landing at Suvla Bay and attacks at Lone Pine, the Nek and Chunuk Bair broke down. Hamilton was replaced by Monro in October, and the Allies evacuated Anzac and Suvla in December 1915 and Helles in January 1916.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Skinner judges that Hamilton's failure to define clear objectives and to supervise Stopford's corps at Suvla wasted his last chance of an operational victory, and that German and Ottoman leaders were generally quicker to see and exploit opportunities. Britannica lists poor leadership in some cases, faulty tactics including a complete lack of surprise, inexperienced troops, inadequate equipment and a shortage of shells. On the Ottoman side, Esat's decision to give Kemal sole control of the Anzac sector cemented the early defence.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: On the first day the slow advance of the ANZAC gave Kemal time to deploy the 19th Division on the commanding Sari Bair and Chunuk Bair ridges and contain the landing. In August a gendarmerie group under the German major Willmer delayed the inexperienced troops landed at Suvla until Ottoman reinforcements arrived, and Chunuk Bair, taken by the Wellington Regiment on 8 August, was lost to an Ottoman counter-attack two days later.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The campaign ended in an Ottoman victory and an Allied defeat; the Anzacs gained little beyond the positions taken on the first day. The withdrawal was the best-run part of the Allied effort: carried out in stages, it removed the troops with very few casualties, and Skinner calls it well planned and successfully executed.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Losses were very heavy on every side, and in the summer more men were evacuated because of illness than wounds. The straits stayed closed to the Entente for the rest of the war, a key factor in the breakdown of Russia's war effort, although the campaign drew Ottoman troops away from the Caucasus front. Ottoman success encouraged Bulgaria to mobilise in September 1915. In Britain, Fisher resigned as First Sea Lord, Churchill left the government and Asquith's coalition was discredited. Victory restored the prestige of the Ottoman army and made Mustafa Kemal a national hero.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Early naval bombardment, Skinner notes, only spurred the Ottoman defence before any troops landed. Amphibious operations need joint planning, clear objectives and commanders close enough to exploit fleeting chances; at Gallipoli the defenders on the high ground repeatedly recovered before the attackers could press on. The well-run evacuation shows what careful planning could achieve in the same campaign.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Historians remain divided over the strategic merits of the campaign. Casualty figures vary widely because sources define a casualty differently and Ottoman figures are largely estimates, as the ANZAC Portal explains. Britannica dates the completion of the evacuation to 9 January 1916, the ANZAC Portal to 20 January. Memory diverges: in Turkey, official narratives came to centre on Atatürk and his soldiers while the roles of Esat, other officers and the empire's non-Turkish troops faded; Australia and New Zealand made 25 April their day of national remembrance, Anzac Day; and French participation was overshadowed by the Western Front.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Harold Allen Skinner Jr.'s 1914-1918-online article gives the Ottoman and German side, the course of operations, an analysis and the legacy in each country. Britannica gives the Allied decisions, the evacuation and the political repercussions. The ANZAC Portal of the Australian Department of Veterans' Affairs gives the plans, the landings, conditions on the peninsula, the August offensive and the evacuation from the Australian side.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: When war broke out, most people expected a decisive battle in the North Sea. Instead both fleets stayed on the defensive for fear of losing important parts of their forces. Britain's Grand Fleet established a distant blockade that cut Germany off from the Atlantic, stopping ships bound for German ports and seizing raw materials and food, and Germany retaliated against shipping bound for Britain. The German High Seas Fleet could not challenge the larger Grand Fleet without risking severe losses.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: For the Royal Navy, command of the sea was paramount, and so long as the German fleet stayed in port that command was secure; the British welcomed battle on the open sea but not in German home waters, with their submarines and torpedo boats. The Germans hoped to whittle the Grand Fleet down piece by piece. In January 1916 Vice Admiral Reinhard Scheer replaced the cautious Admiral Hugo von Pohl at the head of the High Seas Fleet and sought a more offensive policy.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Scheer meant to lure out and destroy part of the Grand Fleet. Hipper's battlecruisers would steam north toward the Norwegian coast to draw Beatty's battlecruiser force into pursuit, while the High Seas Fleet, following about 80 kilometres behind, closed in to destroy it before Jellicoe's main fleet could arrive from Scapa Flow; submarines were placed in strategic positions. The British aimed to bring the German fleet to battle on the open sea, where they believed their numbers and firepower would tell.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The battle was fought in the North Sea near the Skagerrak, about 97 kilometres off the west coast of Jutland in Denmark. It began on a clear, calm afternoon, but visibility worsened through the evening, with mist and smoke over the sea. The German minefields off Horns Reef offered the High Seas Fleet a way home.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Admiral Sir John Jellicoe commanded the Grand Fleet, with Vice Admiral Sir David Beatty's battlecruisers and the attached 5th Battle Squadron as its scouting force. Scheer commanded the High Seas Fleet, with Vice Admiral Franz von Hipper's battlecruisers scouting ahead. The British fleet was considerably larger. It was the only time the two fleets of dreadnought battleships met in battle.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: The German signal of 30 May to put the plan into operation was intercepted by British listening stations; its exact details were not understood, but its wide distribution showed that a large sortie was coming, and by 10.30 that evening the whole Grand Fleet was at sea, before the German scouting group had left the Jade. On the 31st, because the German flagship's call sign was still being heard from Jade Bay, Jellicoe believed that the High Seas Fleet was still in port; he did not know that the call sign was routinely transferred ashore when the fleet sailed.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Light cruisers sent to investigate a Danish steamer met at about 2.20 p.m. on 31 May. In the battlecruiser action that followed, Indefatigable and Queen Mary blew up. When Goodenough's light cruisers sighted the High Seas Fleet, Beatty turned north and drew the Germans toward Jellicoe. At about 6.15 p.m. Jellicoe deployed his fleet across the German line of advance, crossing the German 'T'; Hood's flagship Invincible blew up. Scheer escaped with a 180-degree turn, ran into the Grand Fleet again, and turned away a second time behind a massed attack by his battlecruisers and torpedo boats. In the night his fleet crossed astern of the British battleships and reached the Horns Reef minefields early on 1 June.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Britannica calls Jellicoe's deployment, ordered seconds after he learned where the German fleet was, the most vital decision of the battle. His turn away from the German torpedo attack, because he overrated its danger, let the fleets separate when the High Seas Fleet was most vulnerable, and he avoided a night action because of the Grand Fleet's weakness in night fighting. Scheer's turn-aways, relying on the seamanship of his captains, and his readiness to sacrifice battlecruisers and torpedo boats to cover the second one, saved his fleet.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The crisis came at about 7.15 p.m., when Scheer's battlecruisers and torpedo boats charged to cover his second turn-away and Jellicoe turned his battleships away from the torpedoes; the battle fleets did not meet again. In the night the Admiralty failed to tell Jellicoe that Scheer had asked for airship reconnaissance off Horns Reef at dawn, and erroneous signals and misunderstandings let the German fleet slip past.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The British lost more ships and men; Britannica calls it the bloodiest day in British naval history, and the German press published the figures in triumph. Yet the balance of power in the North Sea was unchanged: the British still dominated it, and the Grand Fleet was ready for action again the next day. Epkenhans concludes that even if Jutland is called a German tactical victory, it did not change the strategic situation.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The German fleet never again seriously challenged British control of the North Sea, and the blockade, which the Imperial War Museums say contributed to Germany's defeat in 1918, continued. Scheer put to sea again in August 1916 to lure the Grand Fleet into a submarine trap, but both fleets turned back. Scheer and Falkenhayn doubted that submarine warfare restricted out of regard for the United States could do decisive damage, and early in 1917 Germany decided to wage unrestricted submarine warfare from 1 February.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Intelligence gathered but misread or not passed on can waste an advantage: the British learned of the sortie in time, then misjudged where the German fleet was and missed the clue to its route home. The loss of three battlecruisers to exploding magazines showed the cost of weaknesses in design and ammunition handling, and Britannica adds that the German ships were well built and the British shells poor. A fleet whose loss would mean losing command of the sea may accept a smaller result rather than risk everything.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Who won has been argued since 1916. The Germans claimed victory on the losses; the Imperial War Museums and Epkenhans stress that the battle confirmed British naval dominance and did not change the strategic situation. In Germany the battle became a myth, with streets named after it and a Skagerrak Day that faded only in the mid-1960s; in Britain it was seen as a missed chance to annihilate the enemy. The sources give different numbers for the ships engaged.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Imperial War Museums give the overview, the blockade and the result. Britannica gives the plans, the intelligence and the course of the battle in detail. Michael Epkenhans's 1914-1918-online article gives the German side, the question of who won and the German myth. Dennis Showalter's Britannica account of 1916 gives the German debate over submarine warfare that followed.

sources.title: Gallwitz, Max von (Hanns Möller, in German)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Fighting had come to Picardy in 1914, and trench lines formed along the Somme during the race to the sea. The British relieved the French north of the river in the summer of 1915 and inherited German positions that had been heavily strengthened. For 1916 the Allies planned a 'Big Push' to coincide with Russian and Italian attacks; the British wanted to attack in Belgium, but the French insisted on the Somme, where the two armies met.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The Somme was the Anglo-French part of a general Allied offensive meant to overstretch and wear down the Central Powers. When the Germans attacked at Verdun on 21 February, the plan shrank and so did the French share, leaving the British the main role; the attack was launched earlier than planned to help the French. As the senior partner, the French had to be accommodated.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Haig hoped for a breakthrough: the Fourth Army would break in at the centre, the Reserve Army with cavalry would exploit any gap, and the cavalry was to ride through to Bapaume on the first morning. Rawlinson favoured more modest 'bite-and-hold' attacks and had little confidence in a breakthrough; Britannica describes the resulting plan as a compromise suited neither to a swift penetration nor to a siege attack.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The fighting was concentrated on the Thiepval Ridge north of a bend in the Somme and on the Santerre Plain south of it, west of Péronne. The British attacked north of the river, on a front from Serre and Beaumont-Hamel past Thiepval and Fricourt to Maricourt; the French attacked mainly south of it, where the German defences were less developed. Villages and woods such as Guillemont, High Wood and Delville Wood became German strongpoints, and the autumn rains turned the battlefield to mud.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Sir Douglas Haig commanded the British, with Rawlinson's Fourth Army making the main attack and Gough's Reserve (later Fifth) Army to the north; many of the British infantry were inexperienced volunteers of the New Armies. General Ferdinand Foch led the French, with Fayolle's Sixth Army astride the river and later Micheler's Tenth to the south. On the German side, Max von Gallwitz took command of the Second Army on the Somme on 19 July 1916, with the First Army also under his army group until the end of August.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: A seven-day bombardment began on 24 June. It was meant to destroy the German defences and guns and cut the wire so that the infantry could simply walk over, but the guns were spread too thinly, many shells were shrapnel or defective, and the deep German dugouts survived. Allied intelligence had underestimated the German defences, and the long, unconcealed preparations gave away any chance of surprise.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 1 July the British attack failed along most of its front, while the French took their objectives. Haig then turned to limited attacks to wear down the Germans. On 14 July a surprise attack before dawn took the German second position on the southern edge of the Thiepval Ridge; from late July into September, costly local attacks were made against fortified villages and woods. In September Foch organised a renewed offensive by four armies: tanks were used for the first time at Flers–Courcelette on 15 September, and Thiepval fell on 26 September. In October and November the offensive bogged down in rain and mud, ending with the capture of Beaumont Hamel in the Battle of the Ancre in mid-November.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Haig's confidence in a breakthrough shaped the plan: he overruled Rawlinson's preference for a short advance and, despite warnings, stretched his guns by setting distant objectives. Britannica, drawing on the British Official History, judges that headquarters did not appreciate that the task was one of 'storming a fortress'. The National Army Museum argues that once the battle had begun Haig had no option but to fight on while the French were under pressure at Verdun, and Philpott credits Foch with coordinating French and British operations after 1 July.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The first morning decided the shape of the battle. The British infantry could not cross no-man's-land before the barrage lifted, and German machine guns and artillery stopped most of the attack, while the French south of the river, with more heavy artillery and more effective artillery-centred tactics, took their objectives. The capture of Thiepval on 26 September, with a concentrated bombardment and new assault tactics, showed how far British methods had improved.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The offensive ended on 18 November with an advance of about 12 kilometres and no breakthrough. Losses were vast on both sides. The German army suffered losses it could not afford and a serious crisis of morale, and never fully recovered from the loss of experienced junior and non-commissioned officers.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: In spring 1917 the Germans withdrew to the shorter Hindenburg Line, a result of the manpower shortage caused by the Somme. The battle relieved pressure on the French at Verdun. The British army that emerged was more professional, and tactics such as the creeping barrage and the tank laid foundations for Allied success in 1918. Heavy losses among the Pals battalions plunged British communities into grief, and the Thiepval Memorial to the missing became a place of pilgrimage.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Artillery had to be concentrated and coordinated with the infantry; a bombardment spread too thinly could not do the infantry's work for them. Plans and reports more optimistic than the facts cost lives: Britannica notes that reports from behind the front were rosier than the facts warranted. The battle also shows an army learning under fire, from the failure of 1 July to the methods that took Thiepval.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The Somme is central to Britain's 'lions led by donkeys' view of the war, in which the first day stands for futile slaughter; Philpott and the National Army Museum argue that it shifted the war of attrition in the Allies' favour and taught the British army to fight a large-scale war. The sources end the battle on 13 or 18 November, and the scale of German losses is still disputed. Philpott notes that France's major and relatively successful part has been all but forgotten, and that in France and Germany Verdun, not the Somme, symbolises the war of attrition.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The National Army Museum gives the plan, the bombardment, the first day and the debate over success or failure. William Philpott's 1914-1918-online article gives the Anglo-French campaign as a whole, its phases and its memory. Britannica gives the critical account drawn from the British Official History, and Hanns Möller's Neue Deutsche Biographie entry (in German) gives Gallwitz's command.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After the retreats of 1915 the Eastern Front was quiet over the winter. Falkenhayn turned to the Western Front, and Conrad concentrated on Italy, which he called 'the true enemy', moving some of his best divisions from Galicia and leaving fortified positions in the east manned largely by raw recruits. In Russia the war minister Polivanov rebuilt the army's supply, training and junior officer corps.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: A Russian attack at Lake Naroch in March to draw German strength from Verdun failed at great cost. When the Austro-Hungarian offensive in the Trentino threatened Italy in May, the Italians appealed to Russia, and the Russians brought their timetable forward. The main blow was to be struck by Evert's armies in the centre, with Brusilov's Southwestern Front making a supposedly diversionary attack.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Brusilov offered to attack along his whole front from Kovel to Czernowitz with all four of his armies, to draw Austro-Hungarian reserves away from Italy; Evert's attack was to follow ten days later. Britannica notes that Brusilov's attack, meant as a diversion, became by far the more important operation.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The Southwestern Front ran for about 480 kilometres from the Kovel and Lutsk area in the north, through Tarnopol and Buchach, to Czernowitz near the Romanian border. The broad spaces of the Eastern Front stretched the lines thin. Behind the Russian front, poor lateral communications and an undeveloped supply network limited how fast reserves could move.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Brusilov's four armies, from north to south the Eighth under Kaledin, the Eleventh under Sakharov, the Seventh and the Ninth under Lechitski, faced Austro-Hungarian armies and the mixed Austro-German Südarmee in deep, hardened positions, with nearly equal manpower and firepower. Conrad, commanding the Austro-Hungarian army, had sent his best units to the Trentino offensive. Alekseyev was the Russian chief of staff.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Brusilov's troops dug assembly areas behind ramparts, communication trenches and saps to within about 60 metres of the Austrian lines, and rehearsed their assaults on replicas built from aerial photographs. Commanders chose attack sectors from the photographs, painted false trenches and built dummy batteries to hide them. Volkov stresses that the attack struck many points rather than one, with short bombardments and approaches made by night.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Brusilov struck on 4 June after short bombardments; on the 5th Kaledin's army attacked toward Lutsk, the defences crumbled and the Russians pushed between two Austrian armies. Austrian commanders fed their reserves piecemeal into each gap and lost them. By 10 June Lutsk had fallen, and in the south the Russians took Czernowitz and reached the Carpathians. German reinforcements arrived from mid-June and a counterstroke by Linsingen checked the advance at Lutsk; renewed Russian attacks in July and August, including the Guards Army's attempt on Kovel, stalled, and by early September the chance had gone.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Brusilov's choice to attack on a broad front, with thorough preparation, short bombardments and many attack points, denied the Austrians a single place to send their reserves. The failure of Evert and Kuropatkin to attack as agreed, and the poor Russian lateral railways, let the Germans move reserves south. Conrad's earlier decision to send his best divisions to Italy had left the line in the east weakly held.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The collapse of the Austrian Fourth Army near Lutsk in the first days opened the front. The arrival of German divisions from 14 June, and German officers taking over Austro-Hungarian units, turned the battle: without surprise, heavy artillery or time to dig forward, the Russian commanders fell back on the costly methods of 1914.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The offensive regained nearly all the ground lost on the Southwestern Front in 1915, drove the Austrians from Bukovina and much of eastern Galicia and took very large numbers of prisoners; Dowling writes that it virtually ended the Habsburg military effort. Russian losses were also enormous, and many of them were deserters or prisoners.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The Germans had to move divisions from the Western Front, where they were needed at Verdun and on the Somme, and Conrad withdrew divisions from Italy. Hindenburg and Ludendorff took command of the whole Eastern Front, and German officers came to control Austro-Hungarian units. The offensive hastened Romania's entry into the war on 27 August, followed by a rapid Romanian defeat. The losses, the Romanian campaign and mutinies in December 1916 broke the Imperial Russian Army, and Britannica writes that the offensive's ultimate achievement was to sound the death knell of the Russian monarchy.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Surprise and preparation could break a strong defence even without overwhelming firepower, and attacking on a broad front kept the defender guessing. But a breakthrough needs reserves and transport to exploit it; without them the advance slowed and the defender recovered. Volkov notes that many of Brusilov's methods remained in wide use in the Second World War.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Historians disagree about Brusilov himself: some see him as an outstanding commander responsible for Russia's greatest victory of the war, while critics argue that several commanders prepared the operation and that his name is undeservedly attached to it. The sources date the end differently: Britannica says the chance was lost by early September, Dowling has the offensive peter out in mid-August, and Volkov dates it from May to August.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Dennis Showalter's Britannica account of the Eastern Front in 1916 gives the Allied context, the course of the offensive and its results. Timothy Dowling's 1914-1918-online article on the Eastern Front gives Brusilov's preparations, the Austrian collapse and the consequences for both empires. Evgenii Volkov's 1914-1918-online biography of Brusilov gives his career, his methods and the debate over his reputation.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Italian and Austro-Hungarian forces had been stalemated on the Isonzo for two and a half years. In the Eleventh Battle of the Isonzo, from August 1917, Capello's Second Army took much of the Bainsizza Plateau north of Gorizia. By the end of the fighting the Austro-Hungarian command concluded that it could not repel another Italian attack.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Austria-Hungary asked Germany for help. The Germans at first regarded the Italian front as secondary, but feared an Austro-Hungarian collapse; in Ludendorff's words, it became necessary to attack Italy to prevent it. With Russia not yet out of the war and the British attacking in Flanders, he could spare only his small general reserve. It was the first time the Germans sent help to their ally on the Italian front.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The aim was to force the Italians back and relieve the weakened Austro-Hungarian army. An Austrian plan for a breakthrough at Tolmino was expanded under Ludendorff: the new Fourteenth Army would penetrate the Julian Alps on a line from the Rombon and Bovec area past Tolmino, with Caporetto roughly opposite the middle, while Boroević's armies advanced on the Bainsizza and near the Adriatic. The planners expected the left of Capello's Second Army to be weak.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The attack crossed the mountain barrier of the Julian Alps on the upper and middle Isonzo, between Plezzo (Bovec) and Tolmino (Tolmin), with Caporetto (Kobarid) in the valley. Beyond the mountains lay the plain of Friuli with Cividale and Udine, and further west the rivers Tagliamento and Piave. Guns had to be brought up mostly by hand and at night, and supplies on pack animals.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The Fourteenth Army of German and Austro-Hungarian divisions was commanded by Otto von Below, with Konrad Krafft von Dellmensingen, an expert in mountain warfare, as chief of staff; Boroević's Austrian armies attacked further south. Luigi Cadorna, chief of staff and supreme commander, led the Italian army, and Luigi Capello commanded the Second Army opposite the breakthrough. Among the German officers was Erwin Rommel, whose striking successes at Caporetto and in the capture of Longarone brought him promotion to captain in January 1918.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: The concentration went undiscovered, thanks to careful precautions and limited Italian air reconnaissance; the Germans hid the Fourteenth Army's arrival and did not fire ranging shots in advance. On 18 September Cadorna ordered the army onto the defensive and repeated the order a month later, but his directives were vague and their execution was not checked; Capello ignored them and underestimated the warnings of an imminent attack.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: At 2 a.m. on 24 October an intense bombardment with high explosive and gas cut Italian communications. In fog, small, independent platoons infiltrated deep behind the Italian lines and seized the heights; some troops advanced 25 kilometres on the first day. Cividale fell on the 27th and Udine on the 28th, and the attackers reached the Tagliamento by the end of the month. Cadorna ordered a retreat, and by 9 November all Italian forces were behind the Piave. Austro-German attacks on the Piave and Monte Grappa went on until the snows ended them on 19 December.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: The Austro-German planners chose surprise and infiltration over a long bombardment and struck where they expected the Italian defence to be weakest. On the Italian side, Cadorna's unclear defensive orders, Capello's failure to follow them, the lack of trained reserves and the absence of any plan for a retreat left the front unable to react; Grillini notes that the first orders went out many hours after the line broke. Cadorna then saved his wings by a precipitate retreat to the Piave.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The cutting of Italian communications in the first hours, and infiltration behind the lines, broke the front between Plezzo and Tolmino on 24 October; with the attackers on the mountains overlooking Friuli, the Italian position east of the Isonzo could not be held. The Italian stand on the Piave, where the invaders had outrun their transport, ended the advance.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Caporetto remains the worst defeat in the history of the Italian army. Very large numbers of Italian soldiers were captured, and the stream of retreating men became a symbol of the battle. The Italians held on the Piave, covering Venice; the attackers, surprised by their own success, lacked the forces to exploit it fully.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Cadorna was replaced by Armando Diaz on 9 November; Grillini notes that the new government of Vittorio Emanuele Orlando had already decided on the change. French and British divisions came to Italy's aid, and the Allied conference at Rapallo led to the Supreme War Council at Versailles and, eventually, a unified command. Britannica judges that Caporetto damaged Italy but also brought a change of command and a reorganised home front, and that the Central Powers' victory was ephemeral because the attack lacked a strategic context.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Surprise, a short and intense bombardment and infiltration by small units could break a front that relied on rigid lines and slow communications. A defence without depth, reserves or a plan for retreat collapses quickly once its communications are cut. A victory in a secondary theatre does not change a war's course unless it serves a wider strategy.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: On 27 October Cadorna issued a report accusing the Second Army of surrendering to the enemy without fighting, while Grillini's account places much of the responsibility on the Italian command itself. The sources describe the bombardment differently: Grillini stresses that it was short and intense, with gas, while Britannica describes four hours of shelling with gas followed by an hour of general bombardment. They also date the end of the battle differently and give different numbers of prisoners.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Anna Grillini's 1914-1918-online article gives the preparation, the infiltration tactics, the Italian command failures and the aftermath. Britannica gives the German planning, the course of the offensive and its consequences. The Holocaust Encyclopedia of the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum gives Rommel's part.

sources.publisher: 1914-1918-online. International Encyclopedia of the First World War

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: The Belgian city of Ypres sat in a salient that had been fought over since 1914 and gave its name to three major battles; the third, in 1917, was the largest. The British had wanted to attack in Flanders in 1916 but joined the French on the Somme instead. In the spring of 1917 a large French offensive failed and parts of the French army mutinied, and after the British offensive at Arras Field Marshal Sir Douglas Haig decided that the British Army would make the next major effort, from the Ypres salient.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Germany had resumed unrestricted submarine warfare, and the U-boats operated in part from ports on the Belgian coast. Haig had to win the war cabinet's approval in London in June. Britannica records that Prime Minister David Lloyd George feared heavy casualties that would be hard to replace, that Haig did not pass on his own staff's warnings about the ground and the weather, and that Admiral Sir John Jellicoe's warning that the war could not go on without capturing the submarine bases helped bring the cabinet round.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Haig meant to take the high ground around Ypres, including the Passchendaele ridge, break through, and advance to the Belgian coast to eliminate the submarine bases. He expected an early breakthrough and told his army commanders that there might be opportunities to use cavalry in masses; the National Army Museum notes that he believed such a breakthrough would win the war.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The Ypres area was reclaimed marshland. British headquarters knew that it would revert to swamp if prolonged bombardment destroyed its drainage, and its intelligence staff found that the Flanders weather usually broke early in August. The attack went in across a bare plain, so the preparations were in full view of German observers. Abnormally heavy rain and the shelling turned the battlefield into a quagmire of water-filled craters, which hampered the attackers far more than the defenders and made it almost impossible to move men, guns and supplies.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Haig's offensive was launched by the Fifth Army under General Sir Hubert Gough and the Second Army under General Sir Herbert Plumer, with a French contingent, against the German Fourth Army in the army group of Crown Prince Rupprecht of Bavaria. It was the largest army Britain had fielded and included Australian, New Zealand, Canadian, South African and other Dominion and imperial troops; the Canadian Corps was commanded by Lieutenant-General Sir Arthur Currie. The German defence rested on concrete pillboxes and specialist counter-attack formations.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: On 7 June Plumer's Second Army took the Messines Ridge south of the salient in a strictly limited attack prepared for a year, helped by the surprise of huge mines fired at the same moment. The main offensive followed nearly two months later. The Germans regarded an attack at Ypres as certain and judged its pattern accurately, and by early July Rupprecht was satisfied that he had enough troops and ammunition to meet it; a two-week bombardment gave further warning.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The attack began at 3.50 a.m. on 31 July. On the left the objectives, including Pilckem Ridge, were taken, but on the vital right the attack failed, and afternoon rain blinded the artillery observers so that German counter-attacks retook ground. The next major attack, at Langemarck on 16–18 August, also failed. Plumer's army then took the leading role: in drier weather, limited attacks on 20 September (Menin Road), 26 September (Polygon Wood) and 4 October (Broodseinde) drove the Germans back toward the top of the ridge. Deeper attacks in rain on 12 and 22 October failed. The Canadian Corps attacked from 26 October, occupied the site of Passchendaele village on 6 November and took the remaining high ground on 10 November, when Haig halted the offensive.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: The sources disagree about the opening plan. Spencer Jones writes that Haig rejected the careful, methodical offensive Plumer proposed in favour of a more ambitious operation under Gough; Britannica says Gough favoured a step-by-step approach for the first day and Plumer urged going all out, and that Haig agreed with Plumer. Either way Haig counted on an early breakthrough. After Gough's repeated attacks gained little, he gave Plumer the leading role for the limited attacks of September. In October, with the weather breaking, he ordered deeper objectives and kept the offensive going; Currie protested at the order to attack Passchendaele but then prepared methodically, building roads, tramlines and gun positions before he attacked.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The rain that began on the first afternoon decided the course of the battle: on destroyed drainage the ground became a swamp, and a rapid breakthrough became virtually impossible. Plumer's limited attacks under overwhelming artillery support, known as bite and hold, won ground and broke up German counter-attacks in late September; Britannica notes that the farthest objective on 20 September was less than 1.6 kilometres deep. Haig took these successes as a sign that the enemy was close to collapse, and the deeper attacks of October failed in the mud.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The British took the high ground around Ypres and advanced about 8 kilometres, but they came no nearer to the coast, and the offensive did not remove the U-boat threat. Both sides suffered very heavy losses in a battle of attrition. Haig regarded it as a success that had brought the German armies closer to destruction, although it was not the breakthrough he had sought.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: In the spring of 1918 the British gave up the Passchendaele ridge without a fight before the German offensive. Jones notes that a German General Staff appreciation judged that the losses in Flanders had brought Germany to the brink of destruction, and that during the battle the German army had turned to an elastic defence based on shell craters and concrete bunkers. Lloyd George later condemned the campaign, and Passchendaele became the symbol of the suffering of the Western Front and the centre of British and Commonwealth commemoration at Ypres, where the Menin Gate records soldiers who have no known grave.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Limited objectives within the range of massed artillery won ground and defeated counter-attacks where deep objectives did not. A plan that relies on surprise and on rapid movement cannot succeed on ground known to flood, attacked in full view of the defender. Above all, the battle shows the cost of persisting after the conditions for success have gone, when optimistic assessments of enemy morale replace evidence.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Jones notes that the historiography of Third Ypres remains especially controversial and divided on whether the British Army conducted the offensive appropriately. The National Army Museum asks whether the gains were worth the cost and whether the battle should have been stopped earlier; Britannica stresses that Haig's assurances about German losses and morale were not borne out. The Canadian War Museum argues that the more populous Allies could better absorb such losses, and Jones cites the German General Staff's own view of its losses. The sources give different casualty figures for both sides, and they disagree on whether Gough or Plumer favoured the more cautious plan.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The National Army Museum gives the course of the offensive, Plumer's bite-and-hold method and the debate over its cost. Spencer Jones's 1914-1918-online article gives the strategic aims, the command changes, the German defence and the historiography. Britannica gives the planning, the cabinet's decision, the ground and weather, and the Canadian attack. The Canadian War Museum gives Currie's objection, preparations and assault.
