sources.title: The Fighting Tactics of the Battle of Cambrai

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Seeing that tanks were useless in the Flanders swamps, officers of the British Tank Corps looked for ground where they could succeed. Their chief staff officer, Colonel J. F. C. Fuller, drew up a plan for a large raid into a pocket of rolling downland south-west of Cambrai, enclosed by canals, where a swarm of tanks would attack without any preparatory bombardment. With Passchendaele showing the need for new tactics, the British command adopted the scheme.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The command turned the raid into a full offensive with far-reaching aims, including the capture of Cambrai and a thrust toward Valenciennes, partly to relieve pressure on the French front. Britannica notes that the resources for those aims had been drained by Passchendaele. Cambrai was a German-held railhead behind the Hindenburg Line.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The attack was to break the Hindenburg Line on a front of about 16 kilometres some 13 kilometres west of Cambrai and encircle the town. It was planned as an all-arms battle of tanks, cavalry, aircraft, artillery and infantry, with the cavalry to exploit any breakthrough.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Unlike Flanders, the rolling downland of the sector suited tanks. The Hindenburg Line had three lines of defences with wide ditches, so many tanks carried fascines, bundles of brushwood, to fill them for tanks and infantry to cross.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: General Sir Julian Byng's Third Army made the attack, with the largest number of tanks yet assembled, five cavalry divisions and squadrons of the Royal Flying Corps; at the point of attack the British heavily outnumbered the defenders. The sector was held by the German Second Army under General Georg von der Marwitz.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: The tanks were brought up by rail and moved into position at night to escape German air reconnaissance, and cloudy weather limited flying by day. The artillery did not register its targets beforehand, so that the barrage would come as a surprise, in keeping with Fuller's idea of attacking without warning.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: At dawn on 20 November a brief, intense bombardment fell on the whole front, and the tanks advanced with the infantry behind a creeping barrage while aircraft attacked trenches, convoys and gun positions. All three lines of the Hindenburg defences were penetrated and some units advanced about 8 kilometres, taking several villages and many prisoners. By evening more than half the tanks were out of action. Progress slowed in heavy fighting, and by 28 November the British held a salient on the crest of Bourlon Ridge; the offensive was halted the next day. On 30 November the German Second Army struck both flanks of the salient. In the north the attack was held; in the south it broke through, and a counter-attack by the Guards Division and then a tank brigade averted disaster. By 5 December the British had been driven back almost to their starting line.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: The British command's decisive choice was to turn a raid into an offensive with distant objectives without the reserves to pursue them; no adequate reserves were set aside to exploit a breakthrough, because so many troops were committed at Passchendaele. The German command answered on 30 November with intense artillery, mortars, gas and infiltrating storm troops against the flanks of the salient rather than its point.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The first morning decided what the attack could achieve: it broke deep into the defences at little cost, but tank breakdowns and losses, bad weather that kept the cavalry from exploiting, isolated units and poor communications left the gap unexploited. The German counter-stroke of 30 November then reversed most of the gains, although it too lost momentum when reinforcements and supplies could not be brought up and its command and communications broke down.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The British kept only the ground they had taken around Havrincourt, Ribécourt and Flesquières, and losses on the two sides were about equal. The Imperial War Museums judge that the battle had little strategic effect on the fighting on the Western Front.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Cambrai was the first large-scale massed use of tanks and aircraft in battle, and it showed that the British could break deep into German defences quickly and at relatively low cost. In their tactics both sides foreshadowed the fighting of 1918: the British combination of tanks, unregistered artillery fire, infantry and aircraft, and the German counter-attack by infiltrating storm troops. Both applied these lessons in the following year.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Surprise and the combination of arms could break into the strongest defences; breaking out needed reserves, reliable vehicles and communications that could keep pace with success. Objectives must match the forces available, and an attack launched while another offensive absorbs the reserves can win ground but not hold it.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources weigh the battle differently. Britannica concludes that it showed armour was the key to a decision on the Western Front; the Imperial War Museums stress its limited strategic effect and its place as a forerunner of combined-arms warfare; the National Army Museum stresses the need for better communications to exploit success. They also explain the failure to exploit differently: Britannica points to the weather and late infantry reinforcements, the National Army Museum to breakdowns, the commitment at Passchendaele, isolated units and poor communications. They give slightly different depths of advance.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The National Army Museum gives the plan, the first day, the German counter-attack and the battle's significance. Britannica gives Fuller's original idea, the British command's aims, the forces and the course of the battle to 5 December. The Imperial War Museums give the tanks' preparation, the unregistered barrage, the fighting for Bourlon Ridge and the ground that was kept.

sources.title: German Spring Offensives 1918 (Alexander Watson)
sources.publisher: 1914-1918-online. International Encyclopedia of the First World War

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: By the end of 1917 Russia's revolution and collapsing war effort had freed German divisions in the east, giving Germany a numerical advantage on the Western Front. The United States had been at war with Germany since April 1917 and was training a huge army, and the National Army Museum notes that Germany knew its submarine campaign had failed. Germany had one brief chance to win in the west before American troops arrived in strength.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: General Erich Ludendorff, First Quartermaster General and the German army's de facto commander, began to consider a renewed offensive in October 1917. On the British side, Haig's divisions were under strength; the government would not send more troops, so he reduced the number of infantry battalions in each division, and Gough's Fifth Army held a long front south of Cambrai with comparatively few divisions.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Ludendorff chose an 80-kilometre front from La Fère to Arras held by the British, whom he regarded as less skilled than the French. He hoped to break through at the boundary between the British and French armies, then turn north and roll up the British line, expecting troops schooled only in trench warfare to collapse under mobile war. He refused to set final territorial objectives.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The attack fell north of the Somme between Arras and La Fère and opened in dense fog. Behind the British front lay the rail hubs of Amiens and, farther north, Hazebrouck, on which the British army depended. As the Germans advanced they had to move men, supplies and guns across a shattered landscape.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The attack struck Byng's Third Army and Gough's Fifth Army. The German assault divisions had the best equipment, horses and fittest men and four weeks' special training in infiltration tactics. The French became engaged as the battle developed.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Great care was taken to achieve surprise. The bombardment was a short hurricane of fire aimed at artillery and machine-gun positions, headquarters, telephone exchanges, railways and communication centres, and storm troops were to infiltrate weak points, bypass resistance and leave following waves to mop up.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: At 4.20 a.m. on 21 March the bombardment began, and five hours later the infantry advanced in fog after the British trenches had been shelled and gassed. The British first and second lines quickly fell; Gough's line, lacking reserves, gave way, and by 22 March the Fifth Army was in retreat and had lost contact with the French to the south. By the evening of 23 March the Germans had advanced up to 19 kilometres in some sectors, and panic spread along parts of the Allied front. On 26 March Haig agreed to Foch's appointment to command on the Western Front. By 28 March new Allied troops had checked the advance east of Amiens, and when the offensive ended on 5 April the Germans had advanced as much as 64 kilometres.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Watson identifies Ludendorff's choices as the cause of the operational failure: he set no final objective, missed the British army's dependence on Amiens and Hazebrouck, and, believing the British beaten, reinforced the southernmost army to keep the French away and then dispersed his strength in several directions, reinforcing tactical successes rather than pursuing a goal. On the Allied side, Haig accepted Foch's appointment in exchange for reinforcements.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The breakthrough of 21–23 March did not become a strategic victory. The Germans did not reach Amiens, did not destroy the British army and did not split it from the French, while Allied reserves under a unified command arrived to close the gap. The attackers were exhausted and lacked the transport to turn local gains into a strategic victory.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: It was the largest territorial gain on the Western Front since 1914, and the Germans took many prisoners. Britannica concludes that the Allied lines were bent but not broken; Watson that the Germans captured nothing of value. They were held east of Amiens in an exposed salient.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Ludendorff repeated the pattern. Operation Georgette in Flanders in April failed to take Hazebrouck, although it took the Messines Ridge and much of the Passchendaele salient. Operation Blücher on the Chemin des Dames on 27 May, meant as a diversion, was expanded after its tactical success and brought German troops within 90 kilometres of Paris, but created another salient. The Gneisenau attack on the Matz in June was inconclusive and the Marne-Reims offensive of 15 July failed. On 18 July a French-led counter-attack took the initiative for the Allies. The German army had lost its best troops and had no reserves, while American soldiers arrived in large numbers and the Allies had placed Foch in coordinating command.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Tactical excellence, surprise and infiltration can break a front, but without an operational objective they only use up the attacker's strength; an offensive must aim at what the enemy cannot afford to lose, such as the rail hubs behind the British front. An attack that outruns its transport stalls, however deep it goes, and a crisis can force the defender into a better system of command.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: After the war the offensives provoked bitter controversy in Germany: critics accused Ludendorff of throwing away a chance of a negotiated peace on an operation doomed to fail. Watson weighs his command errors alongside the German army's limits in material, manpower and mobility; Britannica sees tactical virtuosity unconnected to any strategic concept; the National Army Museum stresses exhaustion and the lack of transport. The sources measure the advance differently (the area overrun in Watson, its depth in Britannica and the National Army Museum), give different loss figures, and date the opening of Georgette to 7 April (National Army Museum) or 9 April (Watson).

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Alexander Watson's 1914-1918-online article gives Ludendorff's planning, the course of the offensives and the reasons for their failure. The National Army Museum gives the British situation, the bombardment and infiltration tactics, Foch's appointment and the later offensives. Britannica gives the attack in fog, the British retreat and the Allied recovery east of Amiens.

sources.title: Amiens, Battle of (Stephen Badsey)
sources.publisher: 1914-1918-online. International Encyclopedia of the First World War

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: The German failure to take Amiens in Operation Michael left the German Second Army under General Georg von der Marwitz holding an overstretched salient east of the city. In May Haig began planning a counter-attack there by General Sir Henry Rawlinson's Fourth Army. In July the French and Americans halted and drove back the last German offensive on the Marne, and the exhausted German army lost the initiative.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Foch, now the Allied generalissimo, planned a general offensive of repeated, relatively shallow attacks on different parts of the German line, allowing the Germans no time to recover. Britannica describes the Amiens attack as part of a limited offensive to secure strategic transit hubs, planned to protect the Paris–Amiens railway. At this stage Foch and most other senior Allied commanders expected the war to last well into 1919.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Fourth Army was to break the German front east of Amiens and seize critical points on the Amiens Outer Defence Line beyond it, protecting the city and its railway, while the French First Army attacked alongside to the south.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The attack was made south of the Somme on a front of about 30 kilometres east of Amiens, in fog and morning mist. The German defences were three lines of trenches with poor communications and few good dugouts. Beyond them lay the wasteland of the 1916 Somme battlefield, and the tanks struggled on boggy ground.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Rawlinson's Fourth Army, almost doubled in strength, comprised the British III Corps, the Canadian Corps under Lieutenant-General Sir Arthur Currie and the Australian Corps, with an American division in reserve, most of the Tank Corps, including the new, faster Whippet tanks, and the Cavalry Corps. The French First Army under General Marie-Eugène Debeney was placed under Haig's command, and British and French aircraft supported the attack. Marwitz's Second Army held the front with weak divisions; Badsey judges that the Allies were superior in numbers, equipment and morale.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: The concentration was prepared in great secrecy. Troops moved to the front by night, false radio traffic supported the deception, and a counter-intelligence operation misled the Germans about where the Canadian and Australian assault troops were. There was no preliminary bombardment, so the attack would come as a surprise.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: At 4.20 a.m. on 8 August the British attacked in fog behind a creeping barrage; the French, with fewer tanks, followed at 5.05 a.m. after a short bombardment. The German first lines were taken by 7.30 a.m., and Whippet tanks, armoured cars and cavalry then pushed on to seize points on the Outer Defence Line. By mid-afternoon the Canadians and Australians in the centre had advanced almost 12 kilometres on a front of 22 kilometres, and many Germans surrendered. III Corps, disrupted by a German attack on 6 August, was stopped short of the Chipilly spur. The Canadians gained another 5 kilometres on 9 August and the French took Montdidier on 10 August, but German reinforcements arrived and the attackers moved beyond the range of their guns. By 12 August few tanks were still working and Haig closed the battle down.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: The Allied commanders chose surprise over a long bombardment, and secrecy over a visible build-up, to break the front on the first morning. When resistance stiffened, Haig stopped the battle rather than force it; Britannica notes that Currie urged consolidating the gains. Haig began preparing the next attack further north, in line with Foch's plan of repeated attacks in different sectors.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The morning of 8 August decided the battle: the German front broke, a wide gap opened south of the Somme, and the large-scale surrenders were unprecedented. Once the attack reached the old Somme battlefield and the German reserves, the advance slowed. Badsey notes that coordinating the mechanised break-through proved difficult: cooperation between tanks and cavalry failed, and the Royal Air Force attacked bridges in the German rear rather than supporting the attack directly.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Amiens was a decisive British-led victory. The Canadian War Museum calls 8 August the most successful day of fighting for the Allies on the Western Front, and the Allies took large numbers of prisoners and guns; the Germans held a new line in front of Noyon and Péronne.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Ludendorff called 8 August the black day of the German army. The National Army Museum notes that he and the Kaiser privately concluded that Germany could no longer win, and Badsey that the German High Command accepted soon after that it had lost the war on the Western Front, something most Allied commanders did not see until early October. Amiens opened the Hundred Days, a series of Allied offensives that broke through the Hindenburg Line at the end of September and ended with the armistice on 11 November.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: The battle shows the integration of infantry, artillery, tanks and aircraft into one surprise attack, and how far the British army had improved since 1916: Badsey contrasts Rawlinson's Fourth Army at Amiens with the same commander and army on the Somme. It also shows the value of stopping once returns diminish and striking again elsewhere, rather than pressing a stalled attack.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Badsey calls the casualty figures for both sides disputed, and the sources give different numbers of prisoners, guns, tanks and aircraft. They date the end of the battle to 11 August (Britannica, the Canadian War Museum) or 12 August (Badsey), and differ on who planned it: Badsey has Haig planning a Fourth Army counter-attack from May, while Britannica describes Foch planning an attack to protect the Paris–Amiens railway. Britannica attributes the end of the battle to Currie's urging that the gains be consolidated, Badsey to Haig's decision as German resistance stiffened.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Stephen Badsey's 1914-1918-online article gives the planning, the forces, the course of the battle and its aftermath. The National Army Museum gives the all-arms attack, the scale of the German surrender and the Hundred Days. Britannica gives the deception, the German defences and Currie's part in ending the battle. The Canadian War Museum gives the secrecy, the Canadian advance and the battle's effect on German and Allied expectations.

phases.title: Secret concentration
phases.description: Haig and Rawlinson plan the attack; the Fourth Army is reinforced by night and the Canadians' move is concealed.

phases.title: Break-in
phases.description: A surprise attack in fog without preliminary bombardment breaks the German front; the Canadians and Australians advance almost 12 kilometres.

phases.title: Exploitation
phases.description: The Canadians gain more ground and the French take Montdidier as German reinforcements arrive.

phases.title: Closing down
phases.description: With the tanks worn out and resistance stiffening on the old Somme battlefield, Haig closes the battle and prepares the next attack.

perspectives.name: Sir Henry Rawlinson
perspectives.objective: Break the German salient east of Amiens with a surprise attack.
perspectives.known: The German Second Army was overstretched and its defences poorly prepared.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether secrecy would hold until the attack.
perspectives.constraints: Moving large forces into position without alerting the Germans.
perspectives.decision: He attacked without a preliminary bombardment behind a creeping barrage, with tanks, cavalry and aircraft.
perspectives.forces: The Fourth Army: III Corps, the Canadian and Australian Corps, the Tank Corps and the Cavalry Corps.
perspectives.terrain: Open ground south of the Somme east of Amiens, in fog.
perspectives.logistics: Night moves to the front; the advance later outran the range of the guns.
perspectives.outcome: The German front broke on 8 August; the advance slowed after the second day.

perspectives.name: Sir Arthur Currie
perspectives.objective: Lead the Canadian Corps' assault on the right of the British attack.
perspectives.known: The corps' move had been concealed by a deception operation.
perspectives.uncertainty: How the Germans would reinforce the sector.
perspectives.constraints: Tanks that broke down or were knocked out, and growing German resistance.
perspectives.decision: He attacked on 8 August and pressed on the next day, then urged consolidating the gains.
perspectives.forces: The Canadian Corps.
perspectives.terrain: The ground south of the Somme, then the old 1916 battlefield.
perspectives.logistics: Attacking forces moving beyond the range of their own artillery.
perspectives.outcome: The Canadians advanced about 13 kilometres on 8 August; the fighting grew harder and costlier in the days that followed.

perspectives.name: Georg von der Marwitz
perspectives.objective: Hold the salient east of Amiens left by the spring offensive.
perspectives.known: His divisions were weak and his defences poorly prepared.
perspectives.uncertainty: That a major attack was imminent.
perspectives.constraints: Inferior numbers, equipment and morale, and a front taken by surprise.
perspectives.decision: He brought reinforcements into the battle and formed a new line further back.
perspectives.forces: The German Second Army.
perspectives.terrain: Three trench lines east of Amiens.
perspectives.logistics: Reinforcing divisions sent in from other sectors.
perspectives.outcome: His front broke on 8 August; a new line was held before Noyon and Péronne.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: The British Egyptian Expeditionary Force was formed in 1916 to defend the Suez Canal and advanced across Sinai into Palestine. After two failed attacks on Gaza in the spring of 1917, General Sir Edmund Allenby replaced General Sir Archibald Murray in June. He reorganised the force into three corps, two of infantry and the Desert Mounted Corps under Lieutenant-General Sir Harry Chauvel, broke the Ottoman Gaza–Beersheba line in the autumn and entered Jerusalem on 9 December 1917.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: In the spring of 1918, after the German offensive in France, most of Allenby's British infantry was sent to the Western Front and replaced by Indian units, many newly recruited; the summer was spent training them. Two attempts to reach Amman and cut the Hejaz railway in support of the Arab Revolt failed. On the Ottoman side, the German general Otto Liman von Sanders took command of the Yildirim Army Group in March, with the task of holding Lebanon and Syria and the communications with the Hejaz, but the Ottoman army was depleted by disease and shortages of men and materiel.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Allenby planned to trap the Ottoman armies on the plains around Megiddo, block their lines of retreat and destroy them with cavalry, infantry, artillery, armoured vehicles and aircraft acting together. Infantry would open a gap on the coastal plain north of Jaffa, and the mounted troops would ride through it into the Ottoman rear to cut the routes for supplies and reinforcements.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The Ottoman line ran inland from the coast north of Jaffa toward the Jordan. Behind the coastal plain the defiles of the Carmel range led to the plains around Megiddo; inland lay the Judean hills around Nablus and the Wadi el Fara road down to the Jordan valley, and east of the river the hills of Moab with Es Salt and Amman. The open country gave mounted troops room to manoeuvre, and the cavalry advanced more than 50 kilometres within a day.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The Egyptian Expeditionary Force was a multinational imperial army of British, Indian, Australian, New Zealand and West Indian troops, with French and Arab units fighting under Allenby's command and British and Australian aircraft in support. Chauvel's Desert Mounted Corps was the striking force, with two infantry corps and Chaytor's Force on the Jordan. Liman von Sanders's Yildirim Army Group, drawn from Ottoman armies and the German Asia Corps, was much weaker in infantry, mounted troops and artillery. Mustafa Kemal, the defender of Gallipoli, was at the head of the Seventh Army in Palestine; the Fourth Army held the front east of the Jordan.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Allenby led the Ottoman high command to believe that his next offensive would be launched across the Jordan, while he secretly concentrated his forces on the coastal plain. From early September the Ottomans expected a British offensive and stood on the defensive along the whole front.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 19 September Arab forces attacked the Ottoman lines of communication, and after a hurricane bombardment and creeping barrages the infantry of XXI Corps, British and Indian, broke through on the coastal plain. The Desert Mounted Corps passed through the gap into the Ottoman rear, took Afulah, Beisan and Jenin, and secured Nazareth, Haifa and Samakh; it held the defiles of the Carmel range to complete the encirclement. XX Corps attacked in the Judean hills while Chaytor's Force took the crossings of the Jordan. British and Australian aircraft attacked the retreating columns, most famously on the Wadi el Fara road, and by 21 September the Ottoman forces around Nablus had broken. East of the Jordan, Chaytor's Force took Es Salt and Amman, and the retreating Fourth Army, blocked by the Anzac Mounted Division and pursued by Arab irregulars, surrendered. The mounted troops then advanced on Damascus, which they entered on 1 October.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Allenby's decisive choices were to deceive the Ottomans about where he would attack, to concentrate in secret on the coast, and to use the infantry only to open the door for a deep mounted envelopment, with aircraft attacking the retreat. Kitchen notes that he valued the Hashemite Arab forces fighting on his right flank more for their political than their military weight. Liman von Sanders, expecting an offensive but not where it fell, kept his armies on the defensive and, after the collapse, defended Damascus with what remained.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The break-in on the coast on the first morning, followed by the mounted corps' ride into the Ottoman rear and its seizure of the Carmel defiles, closed the escape routes within days. Air attacks on the columns retreating down the Wadi el Fara completed the destruction of the armies west of the Jordan.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Within days the cavalry had encircled the bulk of the Ottoman army in northern Palestine and taken very large numbers of prisoners; the Yildirim Army Group lost most of its artillery. Kitchen calls Megiddo the war's most successful large-scale use of cavalry on the battlefield, and the National Army Museum notes Allenby's combined use of mounted troops, infantry, artillery and aircraft.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Damascus fell on 1 October, and the advance went on to Homs and Aleppo. On 30 October the Ottoman Empire signed the Armistice of Mudros, surrendering its forces and garrisons and opening the Straits to Allied occupation. Liman von Sanders was recalled, and Mustafa Kemal took over the Yildirim Army Group until 7 November. Kitchen judges that the campaign contributed to the end of Ottoman rule in the Levant but was not the main reason the Ottoman government ended its war: the collapse of Bulgaria, which cut the link to Germany, was decisive.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Deception that fixes the enemy's attention on the wrong sector, a concentrated break-in and rapid exploitation by mobile troops can destroy an army rather than merely push it back. Air power used against a retreating force can turn a retreat into a rout. A weak and under-supplied defender, holding a long line with no depth, is especially vulnerable to such an attack.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Kitchen records the military historian Basil Liddell Hart's judgment that Megiddo was among the most completely decisive battles in history, but notes that the Ottoman army's acute shortage of men and resources explains how a defeat became a rout. The role of the Arab Revolt is debated: Kitchen judges its military effect minimal, while the National Army Museum and the Anzac Portal record its attacks on communications and the political tension over who entered Damascus first, which upset T. E. Lawrence. The sources give different prisoner figures and different dates for the fall of Aleppo and for the armistice.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: James E. Kitchen's 1914-1918-online articles on the Egyptian Expeditionary Force and on Allenby give the army's development, the battle and its assessment. Odile Moreau's article on the Yildirim Army Group gives the Ottoman command. The National Army Museum gives the plan, the commanders and the course of the battle; the Anzac Portal of the Australian Department of Veterans' Affairs gives the deception, the air attacks, Damascus and the armistice; the Australian War Memorial gives Mustafa Kemal's command.

phases.title: Breakthrough
phases.description: After a hurricane bombardment the infantry break through on the coastal plain, and the Desert Mounted Corps rides into the Ottoman rear.

phases.title: Encirclement
phases.description: The cavalry hold the passes and towns behind the Ottoman armies; aircraft destroy columns on the Wadi el Fara road; resistance around Nablus collapses.

phases.title: East of the Jordan

perspectives.name: Sir Edmund Allenby
perspectives.objective: Destroy the Ottoman armies in Palestine rather than push them back.
perspectives.known: The Ottoman armies were depleted and held a long line; his own army was stronger in infantry, cavalry and artillery.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether his newly trained Indian infantry would break the line quickly enough.
perspectives.constraints: An army reorganised after most of its British infantry had gone to France, and two earlier failures toward Amman.
perspectives.decision: He deceived the Ottomans about the place of attack, broke in on the coast with infantry and sent the Desert Mounted Corps deep into their rear.
perspectives.forces: The Egyptian Expeditionary Force with the Desert Mounted Corps, two infantry corps, Chaytor's Force, aircraft and Arab allies.
perspectives.terrain: The coastal plain, the Carmel defiles and the plains around Megiddo.
perspectives.logistics: Mounted troops advancing far ahead of the infantry into country with room to move.
perspectives.outcome: The Ottoman armies west of the Jordan were encircled and destroyed, and Damascus fell on 1 October.

perspectives.name: Otto Liman von Sanders
perspectives.objective: Hold Palestine and Syria and the communications with the Hejaz.
perspectives.known: A British offensive was expected from early September.
perspectives.uncertainty: Where the main blow would fall.
perspectives.constraints: Armies depleted by disease and shortages, weaker in every arm than the British.
perspectives.decision: He stood on the defensive along the whole front and, after the collapse, tried to defend Damascus with the remnants.
perspectives.forces: The Yildirim Army Group of Ottoman armies and German troops.
perspectives.terrain: A long line from the coast toward the Jordan, with few routes of retreat through the hills.
perspectives.logistics: Shortages of men, materiel and transport throughout 1918.
perspectives.outcome: His armies in Palestine were destroyed, and he was recalled after the armistice.

perspectives.name: Mustafa Kemal
perspectives.objective: Hold his army's sector of the front in Palestine.
perspectives.known: The campaign was already unravelling when he arrived in Palestine.
perspectives.uncertainty: Where and when the British would attack.
perspectives.constraints: An under-strength army in a German-led command whose strategy he had criticised.
perspectives.decision: He led the Seventh Army through the collapse that followed the British breakthrough.
perspectives.forces: The Ottoman Seventh Army.
perspectives.terrain: The front in Palestine, with retreat routes through the hills.
perspectives.logistics: Retreat routes exposed to cavalry and air attack.
perspectives.outcome: His army was swept up in the collapse; after the armistice he briefly commanded the Yildirim Army Group.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: When the United States entered the war in April 1917 it had a small army with no combat divisions. General John J. Pershing, commander of the American Expeditionary Forces, resisted Allied pressure to place American soldiers in British and French units and pressed for an American sector of the front under American command. On 10 August 1918 he took command of the new American First Army, and on 12 September it cut out the St. Mihiel salient in its first independent operation, catching the Germans as they withdrew.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: After the German retreat from the Marne in July, Marshal Ferdinand Foch and the Allied high command planned a series of converging, almost simultaneous offensives along the Western Front. After a sharp disagreement, Pershing agreed with Foch to end the St. Mihiel operation and move the First Army to a new sector between the Argonne Forest and the Meuse, where it would attack with the French Fourth Army west of the Argonne toward the rail centres of Mézières and Sedan.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The First Army's mission was to defeat the German forces between the Meuse and the Argonne Forest and advance northward to Sedan, cutting the railway there on which the German armies further west depended.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The sector lay between the dense Argonne Forest, the most difficult natural obstacle on the front, and the Meuse. Montfaucon, the highest point in the region, the heights of Romagne and Cunel, and the heights around Barricourt dominated the ground in between. The terrain was ideally suited for defence, and the Germans had built multiple defensive positions in depth that extended for miles behind their front line.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Pershing commanded the First Army while remaining commander-in-chief of the whole American force, with American corps and French troops under him. Most of his divisions were inexperienced; Grotelueschen notes that their quality varied more than in any other army, and that the American doctrine of open warfare, with distant first- and second-day objectives, was anachronistic. They faced German divisions in strong prepared positions.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: The St. Mihiel offensive closed on 16 September, and in ten days American staff officers had to replace the French troops in the new sector with a far larger American force, a nearly impossible logistical task; Colonel George C. Marshall is credited with much of the planning that brought the First Army into position on time.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The assault began at 5.30 a.m. on 26 September after intense artillery barrages, and the next day the 79th Division took Montfaucon. Some units advanced more than 8 kilometres in the first two days, but German reinforcements arrived, resistance stiffened and the advance slowed; by 3 October the First Army was consolidating its gains, and divisions became disorganised and had to be replaced. Between 2 and 7 October a battalion of the 77th Division, the Lost Battalion, held out encircled in the Argonne. The second phase opened on 14 October and took the heights of Romagne and Cunel. Pershing then handed the First Army to General Hunter Liggett, who halted the piecemeal attacks and reorganised. By 31 October American and French troops had cleared the Argonne. The final phase opened on 1 November: V Corps took the heights around Barricourt, the German line broke, and American divisions crossed the Meuse. By 7 November I Corps held the heights above Sedan, and on 10 November the Allies reached Sedan and cut the railway. The armistice took effect at 11 a.m. on 11 November.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Pershing's agreement with Foch to fight two offensives less than two weeks apart, the second some 70 kilometres from the first, created serious problems for the second. In the battle he replaced worn-out divisions and ordered his corps to keep pushing, while doctrine and rigid divisional boundaries isolated units and drained the momentum of the first assault. His decision in mid-October to give up command of the First Army to Liggett, who reorganised it for a methodical renewed attack, made the November breakthrough possible.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: After the first two days the advance slowed against defences in depth and German reserves, and October became a grinding battle. The attack of 1 November, prepared methodically and using tactical and technical improvements, broke the German lines and forced a rapid retreat across the Meuse.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: By the armistice the First Army had advanced about 64 kilometres, cleared the Argonne and reached the Meuse above Sedan, with American divisions across the river. Grotelueschen calls the offensive bloody but successful and the largest and deadliest battle in American history; Forney notes that the final breakthrough helped unhinge the German defences on the Western Front.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Forney writes that St. Mihiel had shown the American army capable of operating as a full coalition partner, and that the bloodier, more controversial Meuse-Argonne muddied Pershing's operational legacy. He credits Pershing with modernising the army, building its staff system on the Leavenworth Staff College and incorporating tanks, aircraft and motor vehicles, and notes that many American commanders of the Second World War served under him. At the war's end Pershing argued against an armistice and for an advance into Germany, a position he later retracted.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Expanding an army rapidly gives it mass but not skill; staff work, logistics and experience matter as much as numbers and spirit. A doctrine that ignores the defender's depth wastes the first assault. Pausing to reorganise and attack methodically can achieve what repeated hurried attacks cannot.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Forney notes that many scholars see the American Expeditionary Forces' very high casualty rate and the attritional fighting in the Meuse-Argonne as evidence of Pershing's naivety or overconfidence, and that others credit American money, equipment and food more than its combat performance for the Allied victory; he argues that both views neglect the work of building the army. Grotelueschen judges the American army not the most tactically or logistically competent on the Western Front, but its numbers and willingness to fight essential to victory in 1918. Britannica stresses the disorganisation of its inexperienced formations. Figures for the forces engaged and for losses are given differently in the sources.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Mark E. Grotelueschen's 1914-1918-online article gives the American army's creation, the agreement with Foch, the course of the offensive and its assessment. Andrew J. Forney's article on Pershing gives his command and the debate over his legacy. Britannica gives Foch's general offensive, the terrain and the outcome. The American Battle Monuments Commission gives the mission and the dated phases of the offensive.

phases.title: Redeployment
phases.description: After St. Mihiel, the First Army moves into the sector between the Argonne and the Meuse in ten days.

phases.title: Opening assault
phases.description: The First Army attacks after intense barrages and takes Montfaucon, then slows against German reserves and consolidates.

phases.title: Attrition
phases.description: Hard fighting in the Argonne and for the heights of Romagne and Cunel; Liggett takes over the First Army and reorganises it.

phases.title: Breakthrough
phases.description: A methodical renewed attack breaks the German lines; American divisions cross the Meuse and reach the heights above Sedan before the armistice.

perspectives.name: John J. Pershing
perspectives.objective: Break through between the Meuse and the Argonne and cut the railway at Sedan.
perspectives.known: St. Mihiel had succeeded, and his army was large and eager but inexperienced.
perspectives.uncertainty: How well his untried divisions would fight in deep German defences.
perspectives.constraints: Ten days to move the army after St. Mihiel, and command of both the whole American force and the First Army.
perspectives.decision: He attacked with distant objectives, replaced exhausted divisions and kept pushing, then handed the First Army to Liggett in mid-October.
perspectives.forces: The American First Army with French troops.
perspectives.terrain: The Argonne Forest, the Meuse valley and the heights between them.
perspectives.logistics: A hurried redeployment of a far larger force from St. Mihiel.
perspectives.outcome: A slow, costly advance in October, followed by the November breakthrough.

perspectives.name: Hunter Liggett
perspectives.objective: Restore the First Army's cohesion and renew the offensive.
perspectives.known: The army was exhausted and its general attacks had become disjointed.
perspectives.uncertainty: How long the Germans could hold their remaining positions.
perspectives.constraints: Worn-out divisions and a tangled front line.
perspectives.decision: He halted the general attacks, straightened the line, replaced worn units and prepared a methodical attack for 1 November.
perspectives.forces: The American First Army.
perspectives.terrain: The heights north of Romagne and Cunel and the approaches to the Meuse.
perspectives.logistics: Time to rest units and organise supply before the attack.
perspectives.outcome: The 1 November attack broke the German line and drove the defenders back across the Meuse.

perspectives.name: Ferdinand Foch
perspectives.objective: Strike the German armies along the whole front at once, allowing them no recovery.
perspectives.known: The Germans were retreating after the Marne, and American divisions were arriving in large numbers.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether the American army could fight a major offensive so soon after St. Mihiel.
perspectives.constraints: Pershing's insistence on an American army under American command.
perspectives.decision: He agreed that the Americans would finish St. Mihiel and then attack between the Argonne and the Meuse toward Sedan, alongside the French.
perspectives.forces: The Allied armies of the general offensive, including the American First Army and the French Fourth Army.
perspectives.terrain: The Meuse valley and the Argonne toward Mézières and Sedan.
perspectives.logistics: The German railways through Sedan as the objective.
perspectives.outcome: The converging offensives pushed the Germans back along the whole front until the armistice.
